notes.b: Freshness is judged by sight, touch and smell, and by the reliability of the seller.
points: Eyes: bright, clear and bulging; sunken or cloudy eyes show the fish is old.
Gills: bright red; grey or brown gills show the fish is not fresh.
Flesh: firm and elastic, springing back when pressed.
Skin and scales: moist and shiny, with tight scales and no bruising or breaks in the skin.
Smell: a mild sea smell; a strong or unpleasant smell means the fish is spoiling.
Shellfish: heavy for its size and alive; mussels should be closed, because an open mussel is dead.
Smoked fish should look glossy; frozen fish should be solid with its packaging intact.
Buy from a reliable, hygienic retailer where the fish is kept on ice, check the sell-by date, and buy fish in season.
The Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority controls hygiene in fish landing and seafood processing, within the food safety system overseen by the Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI).

notes.b: Spoilage is rapid, so fish must be used or processed as soon as possible after it is caught.
points: Oxidative rancidity: fats in the fish, especially the polyunsaturated fats in oily fish, react with oxygen in the air, giving an unpleasant smell and taste.
Bacterial action: a struggling fish uses up its glycogen stores before it dies.
Normally glycogen converts to lactic acid, which is a preservative; without lactic acid, fish goes off quickly.
Bacteria work on the flesh and produce trimethylamine, a strong-smelling nitrogen compound that gives spoiled fish its characteristic odour.
Enzymic activity: enzymes in the flesh cause deterioration even at low temperatures.
Fresh fish is kept chilled, below 5 °C, packed on crushed ice until it is used.
Raw fish is stored on the lowest shelf of the fridge in a covered container, so that drips cannot contaminate other food.
Raw fish is kept apart from cooked and ready-to-eat foods to prevent cross-contamination.
Fresh fish is used on the day of purchase or as soon as possible after it.
Covering the fish stops it drying out and absorbing the smells of other food.

notes.b: Freezing stops microbial growth and inactivates enzymes, because the water in the flesh is held as ice.
points: Freeze only very fresh fish; freezing cannot improve fish that is already poor in quality.
Turn the freezer to its fast-freeze setting 3 to 4 hours before freezing the fish.
Freeze fish in usable quantities, so that only the amount needed is thawed.
Do not freeze more than about a tenth of the freezer's capacity in any 24 hours, so that the food already frozen stays frozen.
Wrap fish tightly in moisture-proof packaging or vacuum pack it, to prevent freezer burn and oxidation.
Label each package with the name of the fish and the date.
Store frozen fish at −18 °C or below.
Thaw frozen fish in the fridge and do not refreeze it once thawed.

keyTerms.definition: The deterioration of fish fats when they react with oxygen in the air, producing an unpleasant smell and taste.
A strong-smelling nitrogen compound produced by bacteria acting on fish flesh, which gives spoiled fish its odour.
A stored carbohydrate in fish muscle that normally converts to lactic acid after death, helping to preserve the flesh.
A preservative acid formed from glycogen in the flesh of freshly caught fish.
The action of enzymes in the flesh that breaks down the fish and causes deterioration, even at low temperatures.
Freezing food quickly at a very low temperature so that small ice crystals form and the food keeps its quality.
Drying and discolouration of the surface of frozen food caused by poor packaging that lets in air.
The transfer of bacteria from raw food to cooked or ready-to-eat food.

factCards.term: Five signs of fresh whole fish
factCards.definition: Bright, bulging eyes; bright red gills; firm, elastic flesh; moist, shiny skin with tight scales; and a mild sea smell.
Oxidative rancidity, bacterial action and enzymic activity.

factCards.term: Four rules for freezing fresh fish
factCards.definition: Freeze only very fresh fish; use the fast-freeze setting beforehand; freeze in usable quantities; and label with name and date.

factCards.term: Two effects of freezing on the quality of fish
factCards.definition: Texture may change as ice crystals form, and some B vitamins may be lost.

factCards.term: Two checks on shellfish when buying
factCards.definition: Shellfish should be alive, and mussels should be closed.

questions.prompt: Outline four guidelines to follow when buying fresh fish.
questions.model: Any four of: eyes bright and bulging; gills bright red; flesh firm and springing back when pressed; skin moist and shiny with tight scales and no bruising; mild sea smell; shellfish heavy for its size and alive, with mussels closed; buy from a reliable hygienic retailer where the fish is kept on ice; check the sell-by date; buy fish in season.

questions.prompt: Explain three causes of fish spoilage and describe how freezing fresh fish, when carried out correctly, slows or stops that spoilage.
questions.model: Oxidative rancidity: fish fats react with oxygen in the air, causing an unpleasant smell and taste; oily fish is especially affected. Bacterial action: after death the fish has used up its glycogen, so lactic acid is not formed to preserve it; bacteria then work on the flesh and produce trimethylamine, a strong-smelling compound. Enzymic activity: enzymes in the flesh cause deterioration even at low temperatures. Freezing: the fish must be very fresh and frozen quickly, using the fast-freeze setting, so that small ice crystals form. Freezing at a low temperature, held at −18 °C or below, stops microbial growth and inactivates enzymes, as the water is held as ice. Wrapping in moisture-proof packaging or vacuum packing prevents freezer burn and reduces oxidation. The fish should be labelled with name and date, and thawed in the fridge without being refrozen.
